segments.title: Sub-10,000-ton carriers as working fleet assets
segments.body: The proposal gives Japan a sub-10,000-ton carrier with about 24 aircraft, divided between reconnaissance and fighter duties. Its capacity would be limited, but those missions do not require the air group of a strike carrier. HMS Hermes was only a little over 10,000 tons and provided a practical design precedent. The Royal Navy expected to answer foreign construction in this category with a modified Hermes design. Better boilers and machinery would make the concept easier to execute later in the interwar period.

evidence.note: Japanese small-carrier counterfactual with a proposed air group of 12 reconnaissance aircraft and 12 fighters.
HMS Hermes as a working small-carrier precedent and the Royal Navy's plan to adapt it with improved machinery.

segments.summary: HMS Hermes provides a design precedent for small carriers with about 24 aircraft devoted to reconnaissance and fighter duties.
segments.question: Could navies make useful sub-10,000-ton carriers for reconnaissance and fighter-control duties?
segments.answerShort: Yes. A modified Hermes-style design could carry about 24 aircraft for reconnaissance and fighter duties while remaining a limited fleet asset.

segments.title: Small carriers free Japan's strike-carrier tonnage
segments.body: The counterfactual makes the small carrier part of fleet design. Once sub-10,000-ton vessels cover reconnaissance and fighter-control duties, Japan's treaty-limited fleet carriers can concentrate on strike power and air-group efficiency. Four carriers of roughly 20,000 tons are weighed against three ships of 27,000 tons, with the extra hull remaining attractive under treaty limits. Leaving the treaty system later would reopen the option of building the larger design in series. A successful minor type could therefore change the size and role of the navy's primary striking ships.

evidence.note: Japanese fleet-carrier size choices once small carriers cover reconnaissance and fighter duties, including the option of expanding construction after leaving the treaties.

segments.summary: Small reconnaissance carriers could let Japan concentrate its fleet-carrier allowance on strike power, with four 20,000-ton ships competing against three of 27,000 tons.

segments.title: Working small carriers could displace Ranger and Wasp
segments.body: A proven sub-10,000-ton category would make compromised intermediate carriers less attractive. Ranger might follow Langley into a non-carrier role, while Wasp's attempt to deliver a very small fleet carrier would no longer solve a unique problem. Hornet is different because she is a full Yorktown-class ship and would probably still be built with her sisters. The resulting force would divide carrier tonnage between large strike ships and small cruiser carriers instead of forcing middle-sized designs to cover both missions. Washington Treaty exemption below 10,000 tons would also let the United States order the smaller type repeatedly without consuming its main carrier allowance.

evidence.note: Ranger and Wasp lose their rationale in the counterfactual, while Hornet remains a full Yorktown-class carrier.
Separate large strike-carrier and small cruiser-carrier roles, with repeated orders possible below the Washington Treaty's 10,000-ton threshold.

segments.summary: Successful small carriers could remove the rationale for Ranger and Wasp while leaving Hornet and the other Yorktown-class ships as the main strike carriers.
segments.question: Would successful sub-10,000-ton US carriers eliminate Ranger, Wasp, or Hornet?
segments.answerShort: Ranger and Wasp would probably lose their rationale, while Hornet would remain likely because she was a full Yorktown-class carrier rather than a compromise small design.

segments.title: Small carriers push navies toward multi-carrier groups
segments.body: Once the sub-10,000-ton design works, Britain, America, and Japan would all have incentives to build it in numbers. Larger fleet carriers become the strike centres, while smaller carriers supply reconnaissance, fighter control, and additional decks around them. One British option is six carriers of about 22,000 tons, with pairs assigned to the Home Fleet, Mediterranean, and Indian Ocean. Four or five small carriers around each pair would allow combinations of one large and one or more small decks for particular operations. The Royal Navy's global commitments would therefore shape both carrier size and group composition. The treaty exemption could also draw France, Italy, the Soviet Union, and South American navies with sufficient funds into a wider carrier race. Multi-carrier tactics could develop earlier as these navies experimented with complementary flight decks.

evidence.note: Competitive small-carrier construction by Japan, Britain, and America, with large carriers becoming the principal strike assets.
Six British carriers of about 22,000 tons distributed in pairs, with groups of smaller carriers available around them.
Earlier multi-carrier tactics and possible carrier construction by France, Italy, South American powers, and the Soviet Union.

segments.summary: A working light-carrier category could multiply flight decks, make major carriers more important, and encourage Britain, America, Japan, and other powers toward multi-carrier tactics.

segments.title: Carrier mobility against island airfields
segments.body: A carrier knows where an island airfield is, while the airfield must first locate the carrier, giving the ship an initiative advantage. One contemporary carrier air group might still be too small to suppress a base whose aircraft can operate from rough strips. Early raids against seaplane bases complicate the comparison because those targets are different from fixed airfields. At Coral Sea, extra flight decks could improve Lexington's prospects, but the counterfactual increases Japanese strength as well as American strength. The comparison separates mobility and surprise from the aircraft numbers required to keep a land base down.

evidence.note: Comparison of carrier mobility and targeting knowledge with the limited striking power of one carrier against a resilient island airfield.
Additional flight decks could help Lexington at Coral Sea, but Japanese carriers would also be more numerous in the same scenario.

segments.summary: A carrier can approach a known island airfield from an unknown position, but suppressing the base requires enough aircraft; extra decks at Coral Sea would strengthen both sides.
segments.question: How would additional small flight decks change early Pacific raids and the Battle of the Coral Sea?
segments.answerShort: Carriers could choose when to strike a fixed airfield, but one deck often lacked enough aircraft to suppress a resilient base; extra decks might help Lexington, although both sides would probably have more carriers.

segments.title: Light-carrier treaty arithmetic and fleet tradeoffs
segments.body: Successful small carriers could lead to a separate light-carrier category in the London Naval Treaty, with rules resembling the division between heavy and light cruisers. Under one proposed scheme, Britain and America would each receive 135,000 tons for light carriers as well as their fleet-carrier allowance. That permits nine 15,000-ton light carriers, while reducing each ship to 13,500 or 12,000 tons permits ten or eleven. These are alternative treaty arrangements within the counterfactual. The same tradeoff applies to large carriers: five ships of 27,000 tons compete with six of about 22,500 tons. The extra hull would be particularly attractive to the Royal Navy because its imperial commitments required carriers in several distant theatres. American and Japanese requirements could place greater weight on the efficiency of each large strike carrier.

evidence.note: Alternative small-carrier treaty allowances and the arithmetic for nine 15,000-ton, ten 13,500-ton, or eleven 12,000-ton ships.
Comparison of full fleet-carrier tonnage choices with Royal Navy global coverage requirements.

segments.summary: A hypothetical light-carrier treaty category turns displacement into a choice between more decks and greater capability per ship, with Britain's global commitments favouring wider distribution.

segments.title: Dominion carriers complicate treaty limits
segments.body: Canada, Australia, India, New Zealand, and South Africa could buy small carriers while the Washington Treaty left ships below 10,000 tons outside numerical limits. A later London treaty would then face completed ships owned by separate Dominion governments. Britain could defend them as anti-submarine, convoy, and maritime-security assets after failing to secure a ban on ocean-going submarines. That rationale fits a cruiser-carrier built for reconnaissance and air defence, not a bare escort carrier. The ownership question shows why an apparently simple tonnage rule could become hard to reverse once several governments had ships in service.

evidence.note: Small carriers bought by imperial governments before London treaty negotiations, with anti-submarine and convoy duties as a British justification for retaining them.

segments.summary: Carrier purchases by the Dominions could preserve extra imperial flight decks through treaty negotiations, especially when Britain presented them as ASW and maritime-security ships.

segments.title: A 5.3-inch US dual-purpose cruiser for carrier war
segments.body: A proposed US 5.3-inch dual-purpose gun raises the choice between mass-producing six-inch cruisers and more powerful anti-aircraft escorts. It could make a Dido-like American design possible, or give an Atlanta-like ship heavier armament. In the Pacific-war comparison, the six-inch cruiser's advantage depends on surface engagements that occur less often than its designers might want. Its heavier shell would also help against shore targets, but the difference is judged insufficient to outweigh the escort's air-defence value. The preference for the dual-purpose cruiser follows the expected balance of missions in a carrier war.

evidence.note: Comparison of a proposed 5.3-inch dual-purpose cruiser with six-inch cruisers and Atlanta in a carrier-centered Pacific war.

segments.summary: A proposed 5.3-inch US dual-purpose gun could support a heavier Atlanta-like escort, changing the tradeoff between carrier air defence and six-inch cruiser firepower.
segments.question: Would a US 5.3-inch anti-aircraft gun have blurred the line between light cruiser and carrier escort?
segments.answerShort: Yes. It could support a Dido-like American cruiser or a more heavily armed Atlanta-like escort, with air-defence value that could outweigh the six-inch gun's advantage in surface action.

segments.title: US and Royal Navy light-carrier build paths
segments.body: The Second London Naval Treaty had removed cumulative carrier limits by 1937, so a response to Japanese light-carrier construction would still have to respect individual ship limits. American industrial potential would need investment in shipyards before it could support an earlier large carrier programme. Additional Yorktown-class ships could bridge the wait for a new light-carrier design, since Wasp was considered an unsatisfactory smaller version. Britain had a more immediate design option in HMS Unicorn, studied as a forward aviation support ship from about 1933. Removing some support functions could turn that design into a light fleet carrier close to the later Colossus class. The proposal rests on the amount of design work already available when new orders become urgent.

evidence.note: The 1937 counterfactual, removal of cumulative treaty limits, investment needed for American shipyard capacity, and extra Yorktown orders.
Unicorn design studies from about 1933 and the proposal to remove support features to create a light fleet carrier close to Colossus.

segments.summary: A 1937 response to Japanese light-carrier orders could combine American shipyard expansion and extra Yorktowns with a British carrier adapted from the Unicorn support-ship design.
segments.question: If Japan began mass-building light fleet carriers in 1937, how could the United States and Britain respond?
segments.answerShort: The United States could expand its shipyards and order more Yorktowns while developing a light carrier. Britain could adapt the existing Unicorn support-ship design, with individual treaty size limits still applying.

segments.title: Industrial potential still requires long-term investment
segments.body: The United States had enormous untapped industrial potential, but building additional carriers required shipyard infrastructure first. Expanding that infrastructure would divert construction capacity from other projects while the larger industrial base grew. In this interpretation, short investment horizons in government and business help explain why so much potential remained unused. The comparison with Britain's dependence on Victorian infrastructure makes a similar criticism of later investment choices. Victorian planners need not have looked indefinitely into the future for their work to outlast that of successors with shorter horizons. Industrial potential becomes wartime output only when resources are committed early enough to build the required capacity.

evidence.note: US industrial potential versus available construction capacity, followed by a criticism of short investment horizons in America and Britain.

segments.summary: An earlier American carrier programme would require new shipyard infrastructure, with competing demands on construction capacity and investment.

segments.title: Earlier British carriers would increase demand for aircraft engines
segments.body: Ark Royal lacked an armoured box, but she still had protection, as did American carriers outside the British armoured-carrier category. That distinction matters when comparing the carrier types Britain could order earlier. More flight decks would increase demand for Fleet Air Arm aircraft and the engines needed to equip them. Earlier engine orders are considered a more likely immediate consequence than the arrival of high-performance naval fighters. Additional hulls would therefore expand demand without guaranteeing a particular fighter design or performance level.

evidence.note: The aircraft-procurement follow-up and the distinction between lacking an armoured box and lacking all protection.
Earlier British carrier construction as a stimulus to engine orders, with high-performance fighter development left uncertain.

segments.summary: More British flight decks would bring earlier engine demand, while the distinction between an armoured box and other protection prevents misleading carrier comparisons.
segments.question: What would additional British carriers without an armoured box mean for aircraft design and procurement?
segments.answerShort: They would probably bring more engine orders before guaranteeing high-performance fighters. Ark Royal and American carriers still carried protection despite lacking the British armoured-box arrangement.

segments.title: Hercules power and the redesign of the Barracuda
segments.body: A Bristol Hercules installation was a credible alternative for the Fairey Barracuda, with versions reaching about 1,600 horsepower around 1939-41 and using two-speed superchargers. Different Hercules variants served different performance requirements. The substitution would require a substantially different airframe shape, particularly forward of the cockpit, because the engine differed from the historical installation. The Royal Navy had considered and requested Hercules engines, but the Air Ministry said the supply was committed elsewhere. Engine standardization around 1936-37 was another possible route, with Hercules among the candidates. The Pegasus already serving in the Swordfish, alongside anticipated new engines, complicated that choice. More power on paper therefore did not settle either the aircraft design or the supply decision.

evidence.note: The proposed Hercules-powered Barracuda and the engine's early development, with the initial horsepower figures garbled in the captions.
Hercules development toward 1,600 horsepower and two-speed supercharging, with variants for different requirements.
A major change to the Barracuda's forward shape and the Navy's unsuccessful request for Hercules engines.
Engine-supply restrictions and the proposed 1936-37 standardization choice between Hercules and the Pegasus already used in Swordfish.

segments.summary: A Hercules-powered Barracuda could draw on a developing 1,600-horsepower engine family, but fitting it would change the aircraft and require an engine allocation the Navy had been denied.
segments.question: What if the Fairey Barracuda had used the Bristol Hercules engine?
segments.answerShort: It was technically plausible, but it required substantial reshaping forward of the cockpit. The Navy had sought Hercules engines and been told their supply was already committed elsewhere.

segments.title: Bomber priorities shape naval aircraft engine supply
segments.body: A contemporary journalist interpreted the Air Ministry's priorities as the result of control by the RAF bomber faction. In his account, successes by the Fleet Air Arm or Coastal Command could divert resources and weaken the case for concentrating effort on bombers. That gave the faction an incentive to restrict competing programmes, including their access to engines. He nevertheless acknowledged the logic of this policy if bombers really could get through and decide wars. His criticism was that concentrating resources this way gambled Britain's force development on a single theory of victory. This is an interpretation from the journalist's papers, and he is not named here.

evidence.note: An unnamed contemporary journalist's interpretation of bomber-faction priorities and his qualified recognition of their strategic logic.

segments.summary: A contemporary journalist interpreted restricted engine access as an attempt by the RAF bomber faction to protect its control of Air Ministry priorities.

segments.title: Dominion flagships multiply imperial fast-ship strength
segments.body: A small carrier could serve as a prestigious Dominion flagship, although the original counterfactual follows a battlecruiser route. Six modern F3-style ships would ease the interwar burden on the Royal Navy's own battlecruisers and place fast capital ships near likely wartime tasks. The notional design combines about 28 knots with nine 15-inch/50 guns and dense subdivision. Raising C turret rather than B turret produces a longer arrangement, with somewhat less armour than Nelson but similarly dense subdivision in some areas. A Force Z deployment could then draw on ships already in the Pacific instead of meeting every requirement from the same British pool. In the Atlantic, these ships' heavier gunfire could threaten Scharnhorst-class raiders armed with 11-inch guns, although German protection and subdivision complicate a one-to-one comparison. The Royal Navy's preference for hunting in groups would make local numerical superiority more likely. Its emphasis on night action provided another way to avoid an even engagement.

evidence.note: Small carriers as status-bearing Dominion flagships and additional Pacific forces available for a possible Force Z.
F3-style ships with 28-knot speed, nine 15-inch/50 guns, raised C turret, and dense subdivision, reducing the burden on British battlecruisers.
Heavy gunfire against Scharnhorst-class raiders, qualified by German protection, and the Royal Navy's preference for night action or numerical superiority.

segments.summary: The Dominion-flagship counterfactual turns treaty allocations into extra fast capital ships for imperial stations, surface-raider hunts, and Pacific reinforcement.
segments.question: How would Washington Treaty Dominion flagships change Royal Navy force generation and a possible Force Z deployment?
segments.answerShort: Several modern Dominion battlecruisers would reduce wear on British ships, provide fast assets for distant operations, and strengthen the hunt for German surface raiders even if Force Z itself drew on Pacific forces.

segments.title: Large ships and VLS reload arguments
segments.body: Reloading a vertical launch system (VLS) at sea raises questions about hull size and weapons handling. A carrier or a battleship-sized hull offers a possible route because of its scale, although placing cells above existing magazines also raises a question about weapon flow. The argument favours larger ships than many recent frigates and destroyers for this role. One proposed explanation for jumping directly to the battleship label is that cruiser terminology carries unwelcome imperial associations. Modern surface ships nevertheless retain many traditional cruising missions in peacetime. The gunboat-diplomacy example connects those missions with the pressure exerted by a large ship carrying more guns. These are arguments for considering larger vessels, without a worked design or VLS cell count.

evidence.note: Carrier size as a possible aid to at-sea reloading and questions about battleship barbettes, magazines, and weapon flow.
The case for larger reload-capable ships, a proposed explanation of cruiser terminology, and the comparison with traditional cruising and gunboat diplomacy.
Larger hulls favoured for at-sea VLS reloading, without a worked design.

segments.summary: Larger hulls offer scope for missile reload arrangements, while VLS placement above battleship magazines raises a weapons-handling problem that remains unresolved.
segments.question: Could very large ships, including carriers or battleship-sized hulls, make at-sea missile reloads more practical?
segments.answerShort: Larger hulls make reload and magazine arrangements more plausible, which is why modern debates often jump from destroyers and frigates to much larger ship concepts.

segments.title: Lexington-class ships split across capital-ship roles
segments.body: The Royal Navy shared substantial battlecruiser design information with the United States and understood the American operational purpose, even though it was not enthusiastic about the Lexington class. A continued programme in the surviving High Seas Fleet scenario would probably split into batches. Some ships could be completed close to the original plan, others converted into aircraft carriers, and later hulls redesigned toward a more capable fighting battlecruiser. The distinction among two-word battle cruisers, one-word battlecruisers, fast battleships, and battleships is an interpretive scheme based on their intended roles. A worldwide cruiser with battleship guns sits at a different point from a ship expected to fight comparable capital ships. Machinery power density also changes the design choices available at different dates, as the comparison of Invincible and HMS Tiger illustrates.

evidence.note: Lexington's future in the surviving High Seas Fleet scenario, British-American design information sharing, and British reservations about the class.
Possible batches completed as originally planned, converted to carriers, or redesigned as more capable fighting battlecruisers.
Machinery power density and the Invincible-Tiger comparison, followed by the carrier eight-inch-gun treaty aside.

segments.summary: The Lexington counterfactual uses British information sharing, machinery density, and the battlecruiser spectrum to explain why one class could produce several different outcomes.
segments.question: What might become of the Lexington class if the German High Seas Fleet survived and the United States continued the program?
segments.answerShort: The class would probably split into batches: some ships completed to the original design, some converted into carriers, and perhaps others redesigned toward the better-protected end of the battlecruiser spectrum.

segments.title: Machinery density shifts the battlecruiser spectrum
segments.body: In this classification, battle cruiser, battlecruiser, fast battleship, and battleship occupy different points on a spectrum of capital-ship roles. The two-word battle cruiser is close to a large armoured cruiser intended to range worldwide with battleship-grade guns, with Invincible as the example. Designs intended to fight comparable capital ships sit farther along that spectrum. The boundaries also change with machinery technology because greater power density alters how much hull space propulsion requires. HMS Tiger could generate much more power than Invincible for a given machinery allocation. A hypothetical Tiger devoting the same proportion of hull space to machinery as Invincible is estimated here at about 32 knots; that is a design comparison, not a claim about Tiger's actual service speed.

evidence.note: The proposed capital-ship classification and a hypothetical 32-knot Tiger with Invincible's proportional machinery allocation.

segments.summary: Invincible and HMS Tiger illustrate how machinery power density changes the space available for a capital ship's speed, protection, and fighting role.

segments.title: Lexington's eight-inch guns and the cruiser treaty limits
segments.body: The Lexington carrier conversions prompt a criticism of their eight-inch guns. In this treaty-based argument, a carrier's heavy gun battery has less justification under Washington rules that permit additional cruisers. Cruiser restrictions under the London treaty make the same choice more understandable. The judgement concerns the gun battery's rationale under different treaty conditions, rather than whether the hulls could become effective carriers.

evidence.note: Criticism of the carriers' eight-inch guns and the distinction between their rationale under Washington and London treaty conditions.

segments.summary: The case for eight-inch guns on Lexington-class carriers changes when treaty rules restrict the alternative of building more cruisers.

segments.title: PLAN carrier learning extends beyond flying aircraft
segments.body: Carrier competence depends on flight-deck and hangar crews as much as on aviators and maintainers. Fuel, food, ammunition, spare parts, and escort composition are further measures of operational maturity. The PLAN's carrier capability is still developing in this December 2025 assessment, with working ideas that remain open to revision. Its effort to acquire information and learn from experience suggests that the eventual carrier-group model is still taking shape. Visible flight operations reveal only part of the personnel and sustainment system a navy must master.

evidence.note: Flight-deck and hangar personnel, fuel, food, ammunition, spares, and escort requirements as dimensions of carrier experience.
The PLAN's willingness to revise its operating ideas and its investment of effort in learning.

segments.summary: The PLAN's carrier learning involves deck crews, supplies, and escort choices as well as flying aircraft, with its operating model still developing in the December 2025 assessment.
segments.question: How much has the PLAN learned about the personnel, logistics, and escort demands of sustained carrier operations?
segments.answerShort: In the December 2025 assessment, it has working ideas about personnel, logistics, and escorts and remains open to revising them through experience.

segments.title: W. D. Forbes and British carrier design work
segments.body: William Archibald Davidson Forbes worked below better-known figures such as Goodall and Henderson and at times directly oversaw the British carrier department. His technical work included an internal-combustion turbine system developed with a colleague to improve engine efficiency. After World War II, he presented a joint paper with Dr. J. Harris in 1946 on underwater paints, fouling, and wartime anti-corrosion work. Forbes was born in Hackney in 1890, the son of a bookseller's assistant, and died in 1980. His career account places an engineering apprenticeship at a shipbuilder in 1911 and Admiralty recruitment in 1920. He then spent the rest of his working life in the Director of Naval Construction's organisation. His background provides an example of the apprenticeship route into naval construction, which could draw people from outside the social circles commonly associated with senior naval careers.

evidence.note: Forbes's full name, position below Goodall and Henderson, and periods overseeing the carrier department.
Internal-combustion turbine research and the 1946 joint paper with Dr. J. Harris on underwater paints, fouling, and wartime anti-corrosion work.
Forbes's 1890-1980 lifespan, Hackney family background, apprenticeship, and 1920 recruitment into naval construction.

segments.summary: W. D. Forbes oversaw carrier design work and contributed to propulsion and hull-protection research, following an apprenticeship route into the Admiralty.
segments.question: Was W. D. Forbes the same person as William Archibald Davidson Forbes, and what did he do?
segments.answerShort: Yes. He was William Archibald Davidson Forbes, an important Royal Navy design figure who worked below Goodall and Henderson and sometimes oversaw the carrier department.
